learningObjectives.title: Feudalism, the Domesday Book and resistance

questions.q: In which month and year did Edward the Confessor die, sparking the succession crisis?
questions.explain: Edward the Confessor died childless on 5 January 1066, leaving no clear heir to the English throne.

questions.q: Which claimant to the English throne in 1066 was the King of Norway?
questions.explain: Harald Hardrada, King of Norway, pressed his claim by invading northern England in September 1066.

questions.q: Why did William, Duke of Normandy, claim the English throne was rightfully his?
options: He claimed Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn an oath to support him
He was Edward the Confessor's eldest son
He had been chosen as king by the Witan
He was already the King of Norway
questions.explain: William argued that Edward had named him heir and that Harold Godwinson had sworn a sacred oath to back his claim.

questions.q: Why was Harold Godwinson's army at a disadvantage when it reached Hastings?
options: It had just marched south after fighting Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge
It had lost all of its weapons
It was outnumbered by ten to one
questions.explain: Harold's men were tired and depleted after defeating the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge and marching rapidly south.

questions.q: On what date was the Battle of Hastings fought?
questions.explain: William defeated and killed Harold at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066.

questions.q: A chronicler describes Harold's housecarls standing shoulder to shoulder on the ridge behind a barrier of overlapping shields. Which English tactic is being described?
questions.explain: The shield wall was the main English defensive formation and was difficult for Norman cavalry to break.

questions.q: How did the Normans' use of feigned retreats help them win at Hastings?
options: They lured English soldiers down from the ridge, breaking the shield wall
They allowed the Normans to flee the battlefield safely
They gave Harold time to bring up reinforcements
They protected the Norman archers from English arrows
questions.explain: By pretending to flee, the Normans tempted the English to leave their strong position, weakening the shield wall.

questions.q: On what date was William crowned King of England?
questions.explain: William was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day, 25 December 1066.

questions.q: What kind of castle did the Normans build quickly to secure control after 1066?
questions.explain: Motte and bailey castles could be raised rapidly from earth and timber to dominate an area.

questions.q: Why did the Normans build so many castles across England?
options: To intimidate and control the local population and act as military bases
To provide places of worship for villagers
To store the records of the Domesday Book
questions.explain: Castles gave the Normans strongholds from which to overawe and dominate a largely hostile population.

questions.q: In 1069-70 William crushed northern rebellions by burning villages, crops and livestock, causing widespread famine. What is this campaign called?
questions.explain: The Harrying of the North devastated northern England in order to end resistance permanently.

questions.q: Why did William create powerful 'marcher' earldoms along the Welsh border?
options: To defend the frontier by granting trusted earls extra land and authority
To carry out the Domesday survey
questions.explain: Marcher earls were given special powers to guard and control the vulnerable border with Wales.

questions.q: Why did William take land from Anglo-Saxon nobles and give it to his Norman followers?
options: To reward loyal supporters and weaken the power of the English nobility
To provide material for the Domesday Book
To defend the border with Scotland
To pay the Pope for his banner
questions.explain: Redistributing land rewarded Norman loyalty while stripping the English elite of wealth and power.

questions.q: Who led Anglo-Saxon resistance to the Normans in the Isle of Ely around 1071?
questions.explain: Hereward the Wake led a rebellion based in the marshy Isle of Ely before it was eventually crushed.

questions.q: In which year was the Domesday Book compiled?
questions.explain: The Domesday survey was carried out and largely completed in 1086.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of the Domesday Book?
options: To record who held land and its value so that taxes could be assessed accurately
To list every battle William had fought
To record all church services in England
To plan the building of new castles
questions.explain: The survey recorded landholding and wealth so William could raise taxes and know exactly what he ruled.

questions.q: In the feudal system, what were the great men who held land directly from the king called?
questions.explain: Tenants-in-chief, or barons, held land directly from the king in return for service and loyalty.

questions.q: Under the feudal system, what did a knight mainly owe his lord in return for land?
options: Military service when the lord required it
A share of every harvest forever
questions.explain: In exchange for holding land, knights owed their lord military service, usually for a set number of days.

questions.q: A Norman baron kneels before the king, places his hands between the king's and swears to be his loyal man in return for holding land. What is this ceremony called?
questions.explain: Homage was the ceremony in which a vassal publicly swore loyalty to his lord in return for land.

questions.q: The king grants a large estate to a baron on condition that the baron supplies a fixed number of knights for the royal army. Which system does this describe?
questions.explain: Feudalism tied landholding to service, with land granted in return for knights, loyalty and military support.
